title: LLM Generated Regression Results vs. Specialized Econometric Software (STATA)
items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) offer unprecedented assistance in economic research, yet researchers often mistakenly trust these tools to perform native statistical calculations on raw data. This paper exposes the mathematical limitations of LLMs and proposes a structured workflow for safely integrating artificial intelligence into econometric analysis. The proposed three-phase strategy enables researchers to use LLMs for conceptualization and code generation while ensuring that all final computations are executed in dedicated econometric software such as Stata. Through a detailed case study involving household income transfer data and quantile regression, this paper demonstrates that LLM-generated statistical outputs can produce fabricated coefficients that contradict empirical findings derived from authentic computation. The results confirm that while LLMs serve as effective cognitive assistants for structuring research designs and generating preliminary code, they cannot substitute for the deterministic mathematical operations required in rigorous econometric analysis. This paper contributes to the growing literature on responsible AI integration in the social sciences by offering a practical, replicable methodology that preserves scientific validity while improving the productivity gains when using AI tools.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>LLM's code generation capabilities have yielded substantial improvements in the effectiveness of programming tasks. However, LLM-generated code still suffers from compilation and runtime errors. Existing offline preference optimization methods primarily focus on enhancing LLMs' coding abilities using pass/fail signals in the preference data, overlooking the deep-level error types in the failed codes. To address this, we propose Adaptively Progressive Preference Optimization (AP2O) for coding (i.e., AP2O-Coder), a method that guides LLMs adaptively and methodically to reduce code errors for code generation. Specifically, we construct an error notebook from failed codes and progressively optimize the LLM to correct errors type by type. Furthermore, we adaptively replay error types to tailor to the LLM's evolving weaknesses throughout training. Through extensive experiments on both code and general LLMs (Llama, Qwen, and DeepSeek series) with parameters ranging from 0.5B to 34B, our AP2O-Coder improves code generation performance by up to 3% in pass@k while using less preference data.</jats:p>

title: Executable but Wrong: Verifier-Grounded Contracts and Counterexamples for LLM-Generated Music Programs
items.abstract:
<jats:p>A generated program can compile, execute, and still be wrong in the only way its user cares about. This is common in creative domain-specific languages: the artifact is partly subjective, yet requests often contain objective promises such as a tempo, onset grid, pitch range, or event count. Ordinary compilers establish executability, while self-critique leaves the model to invent its own oracle.
We present StruSpec, a verifier-grounded workflow for LLM-generated Strudel music programs. It turns explicit promises into bounded executable contracts, evaluates a deterministic Strudel subset with exact rational time and source provenance, and returns typed counterexamples to a preservation-aware repair loop. The model proposes patches; only re-execution and verification can end the loop. We validate the semantic boundary against the official runtime, an independently implemented semantics, generated oracles, metamorphic relations, controlled faults, and reviewed natural programs.
The evaluation separates four questions that are often conflated. Across 4,000 generations, 81.03% compiled but only 15.98% satisfied every hard constraint. On 600 paired failures, localized counterexamples improved strict repair success by 10.83 percentage points with GLM-5.2 (95% CI 8.17–13.67) and by 14.83 points in a protocol-matched DeepSeek V4 Pro replication (11.83–17.84). On a new 192-request, author-confirmed expert population, localized repair also beats generic feedback with both GLM (17 vs. 0 repairs) and DeepSeek (12 vs. 1), although only 67 requests reach a complete-trace semantic violation. A symbolic-first variant used 78.7% fewer model calls and 67.2% fewer output tokens, although its typical successful patch was no smaller. Conversely, supplying the same structured contract before any failure reduced first-attempt satisfaction: 23.17% for direct generation, 18.67% with a gold contract, and 17.54% with a parsed contract. The combined evidence reveals a phase asymmetry: structure is valuable when independent execution turns it into new diagnostic evidence, not when a redundant schema is merely placed in front of a generator.</jats:p>

<jats:p>The object of research is an LLM-assisted process of Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) generation for cloud deployment. The problem is that large language models can convert user requests into syntactically valid IaC, but such generated IaC fails deployment. This occurs because such artefacts often omit required cloud relations or violate policy constraints, inaccurately interpret user intent, or lack rollback logic. As a result, the research proposes a Semantic Infrastructure-as-Code (SIaC) pipeline, where instead of a final IaC, the LLM first generates a candidate infrastructure graph. Further, this graph is completed and validated using ontology reasoning, SHACL/SPARQL validation, and other formal procedures before the generation of the final backend artifact. According to the 60 AWS ECS/Fargate-oriented scenarios that were tested in a LocalStack-based AWS emulation environment, Full SIaC achieved 74.4% sandbox deployment success, compared with 43.6% for direct LLM-to-IaC and 59.0% for LLM+RAG-to-IaC. Compared with the baselines, SIaC improved semantic intent coverage, dependency completeness, and policy compliance. It also reduced invalid dependencies and the need for manual corrections. This improvement is achieved because reliability is checked through an inspectable knowledge graph, not only through prompts and generated text. This graph supports the detection and correction of dependencies, placements, policies, and safety issues before deployment. In addition to higher deployment success, SIaC also provides a more controllable and manageable transformation path from natural-language intent to executable infrastructure.
This method is suitable if the user's requirements can be mapped to the maintained provider ontologies and if the additional time spent on analysis is considered a acceptable trade-off for improved reliability, auditability, and reduced maintenance.</jats:p>

title: DepFailBench: Task-dependent effects of resilience requirements on LLM-generated backend services
items.abstract: <jats:p>Backend services generated by large language models may satisfy clean requests while mishandling downstream failures. We compare baseline and augmented operational contracts in four fixed Python backend tasks: a product proxy, paginated catalog, order payment, and object upload. Two recorded model configurations produced 20 one-shot implementations per task and condition, yielding 320 saved programs. A hardened deterministic harness evaluated clean behavior, scripted errors, timeouts, malformed responses, rate limits, pagination cycles, acknowledgment loss, and finite timeout behavior. The unconditional all-check rate changed by +7.5 percentage points for OpenAI and -13.75 points for Anthropic when averaged equally across tasks. Task-level differences were +30, -5, +20, and -15 points for OpenAI and +15, -5, -55, and -10 points for Anthropic. The Anthropic fixed-task contrast was statistically detectable in the negative direction (Holm-adjusted permutation p=0.0156; bootstrap interval -21.25 to -5.0 points); OpenAI&apos;s was not (p=0.187; interval -1.25 to 16.25). Three hardened executions per program produced zero categorical disagreements. An artifact-level correction ledger records 53 programs that changed from pass to fail under stricter trace, state, and timeout checks. An externally sourced case study then applied the same evidence principles to unchanged Stripe and Seam SDKs: all 18 frozen contracts passed in three repetitions. The results show that operational instructions do not provide a general reliability guarantee; their effects depend on task, baseline, model, and coherent timeout budgeting.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>This work performs systematic studies for code verification for turbulence modeling in our research CFD code SENSEI. Turbulence modeling verification cases including cross term sinusoidal manufactured solutions and a few exact solutions are used to justify the proper Spalart–Allmaras and Menter’s SST turbulence modeling implementation of the SENSEI CFD code. The observed order of accuracy matches fairly well with the formal order for both the 2D/3D steady-state and 2D unsteady flows when using the cross term sinusoidal manufactured solutions. This work concludes that it is important to keep the spatial discretization error in a similar order of magnitude as the temporal error in order to avoid erroneous analysis when performing combined spatial and temporal order analysis. Since explicit time marching scheme typically requires smaller time-step size compared to implicit time marching schemes due to stability constraints, multiple implicit schemes such as the singly diagonally implicit Runge–Kutta multistage scheme and three point backward scheme are used in our work to mitigate the stability constraints.</jats:p>

title: A Two-tier Evaluation of LLM-generated Java Design Patterns
items.abstract: <jats:p>Automated evaluation of LLM-generated code usually reports one number for code quality. We ask what that number actually measures. We build a two-tier instrument for Java and run it on the same generated programs. Tier 1, the Code Quality Score (CQS), combines the Maintainability Index with entropy-weighted Chidamber-Kemerer metrics; it is computed for 996 generated projects. Tier 2, the Comprehensive Quality Score (CompQS), adds a Pattern Implementation Quality Score (PIQS) that checks, with predicate logic over the source structure, whether a program really implements the design pattern it was asked for; it is computed for 60 projects covering five Gang-of-Four patterns and 12 application domains. The two tiers order the same programs differently (Spearman ρ = 0.618). Singleton moves from fourth place under CQS to second place under CompQS, because its code is untidy but its structure is always correct, and Composite is last under both. A quality gate built on CQS alone therefore has no way to register whether the requested pattern is present: structurally incomplete Composite implementations still score as high as 71 under CQS, which looks acceptable. We replicate the comparison on three further open-weight models over a matched grid of five patterns × 12 domains with three seeds, pooling all four datasets into 600 evaluations: PIQS spans 35.9 points across the five patterns while CQS spans 6.8, and Singleton moves from fourth to second. Separately, once identifiers are renamed, the strongest of three models retains 63 of its 83 correct pattern recognitions (75.9%), which suggests that part of what a recognition benchmark measures is naming convention rather than structure. We report both results as evidence about the measuring instrument, not as a ranking of models.</jats:p>

title: Rediscovering Architectural Decision Records: How Persistent Design Context Improves LLM Code Generation
items.abstract: <jats:p>As AI coding tools proliferate, multi-turn development using large language models (LLMs) is becoming commonplace. However, the "context degradation" problem-where design intent is lost across sessionsremains a serious challenge that leads to quality deterioration as projects grow in complexity. This study proposes "sqlew," a tool that repurposes Architectural Decision Records (ADRs)-a practice proposed in 2011 but abandoned due to human operational overhead-as external design memory for LLMs. sqlew realizes automated ADR recording and selective retrieval via structured queries through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), constructing a coexistence model of static instruction (CLAUDE.md) and dynamic rationale (ADR). We conducted a controlled experiment on a 12.5-turn TypeScript workflow approval system development across three conditions: no ADR (vanilla), from-inception adoption (sqlew), and retroactive adoption (Vanilla-to-sqlew, v2s). The sqlew condition reduced development time by 10.1% (496 min vs. 552 min) and total tool calls by 10.8%. In the vanilla condition, a supplementary turn (Turn 12.6: 29 min, 21,751K tokens) was required to compensate for missing E2E tests; including this hidden cost widened the time difference to 14.6%. Keyword-based density analysis of Chain of Thought (CoT) revealed a qualitative shift in reasoning patterns (Trial-and-Error Loop → Context-Informed Reasoning) and accelerating divergence in prior decision reference density (+21% → +64% → +137%). The most striking finding is the compliance gap between instruction and rationale. Despite the same TDD instruction being present in CLAUDE.md, conditions where ADRs contained the rationale for why TDD was adopted (sqlew/v2s) spontaneously generated 16-25 E2E tests, whereas the vanilla condition produced zero. LLMs exhibit higher compliance and reasoning quality toward "why to do something (rationale)" than "what to do (instruction)." We release all session logs, prompts, and analysis code, and invite replication.</jats:p>

title: Causal Sycophancy: Systematic Causal Admissibility Failures in LLM-Generated Explanations
items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) generate explanations that are consistently fluent but not consistently valid. We demonstrate that this gap is systematic, measurable, and cross-architectural. We introduce a constraint-based causal admissibility framework comprising five formal constraints — temporal precedence (C₁), spatial relevance (C₂), mechanistic plausibility (C₃), non-spuriousness (C₄), and completeness (C₅) — and apply it to 40 + 1 multivariant structured urban transportation incident scenarios evaluated across three large language models: Llama 3.3 70B, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and Gemini 3 Pro under zero-shot prompting.,Our evaluation reveals that 52.5% of generated explanations violate at least one causal constraint despite being uniformly fluent and coherent. Violations are systematic rather than random: completeness failures (C₅) dominate at 33%, driven by consistent omission of enabling conditions such as road geometry and environmental context, while mechanistic plausibility failures (C₃) occur in 20% of cases and cluster around scenarios requiring physical world knowledge.,A controlled cross-model experiment reveals a novel phenomenon we term causal sycophancy: the tendency of LLMs to accept and propagate physically impossible causal claims from the prompt in order to maintain narrative coherence. All three models accepted black ice formation at 5°C — a physical impossibility — without qualification. Critically, Gemini 3 Pro’s 45.9-second extended reasoning delay did not prevent this failure, demonstrating that the behavior is architectural rather than superficial. Our findings establish that fluency and causal validity are orthogonal dimensions of explanation quality, and that current LLMs cannot be safely deployed in causal reasoning tasks without external verification. This work builds upon and extends a prior constraint-based diagnostic study in environmental AI (Yahya Khan, 2026) generalizing the evaluation methodology from deforestation attribution to structured transportation incident analysis.</jats:p>

title: From linguistic evaluation to mechanistic verification: testing LLM-generated farm recommendations
items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLM) are increasingly used to generate farm-management advice, but their biophysical consequences remain largely unverified. We introduce a process-based verification framework that combines management portfolios generated by ChatGPT and Claude with the process-based model LandscapeDNDC across 11 contrasting agroecosystems. The LLMs produced agronomically plausible interventions, privileging changes in fertiliser timing, splitting and rates, and generally preserved crop yields. However, their agreement was markedly weaker for environmental targets like nitrogen losses and soil organic carbon. LLMs predicted the direction of agri-environmental change more reliably than its magnitude: directional agreement averaged 86%, whereas only 49% of simulated responses fell within the expected ranges. Portfolios that targeted several targets simultaneously rarely performed consistently across sites. Our results show that process-based models can screen AI-generated farm recommendations for environmental burden shifting before they are used in practice.</jats:p>

               <jats:p>The Monte Carlo method is essential in field of nuclear engineering and has been widely applied in reactor particle simulation owing to the rapid development of computer technology. Academic institutes and organizations of different countries have developed their own Monte Carlo code. title: Multi-Disease AI Diagnosis System Using Minimal Code and LLM-Powered Explanations
items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a novel approach to multi-disease diagnosis using a lightweight neural network architecture combined with large language model (LLM) powered explanations. We demonstrate how modern AI assistants can enable rapid development of functional healthcare AI systems with minimal code implementation. Our system achieves 72% accuracy on synthetic multi-disease classification tasks (Diabetes, Parkinson's Disease, and Healthy classifications) while providing human-readable explanations for each diagnosis through an integrated LLM reasoning module. The complete system, implemented in under 500 lines of code, demonstrates end-to-end functionality from data generation to model deployment, showcasing the potential for democratizing AI healthcare development. Key contributions include: (1) a streamlined architecture combining neural networks with LLM explanations, (2) automatic symbolic rule extraction for high-confidence predictions, (3) a deployable model export system, and (4) transparent documentation of AI-assisted development methodologies.</jats:p>

title: Ethical Considerations of LLM-Driven Quantum Code Generation for Optimization Tasks
container-title: The American Journal of Engineering and Technology
items.abstract: <jats:p>The convergence of large language models (LLMs) and quantum computing has the potential to revolutionize software development for quantum optimization tasks. AI-assisted code generation, powered by models like OpenAI Codex, can accelerate the design of quantum algorithms by automating routine coding tasks and democratizing access to quantum programming. However, this innovation introduces a web of ethical, legal, and technical challenges. This paper investigates the implications of using LLMs to generate quantum code, focusing on intellectual property (IP) concerns, the risk of unintended outcomes, legal ambiguity, and dual-use scenarios. We propose an ethical architecture for responsible AI-assisted development, incorporating human-in-the-loop systems, license-compliance mechanisms, and auditing tools. Case studies illustrate potential failures in code correctness, security, and attribution. We conclude with recommendations for explainable AI systems, curated datasets, and governance models that ensure innovation without sacrificing safety or compliance. By addressing these concerns proactively, the community can guide LLM-powered quantum development toward a responsible future.</jats:p>

title: Enhancing Consumer behavior Prediction with LLM-generated Data: A Signal Combination Approach
items.abstract: <jats:p>The dominant approach to using large language models in behavioral research treats AI responses as direct substitutes for human data, requiring accuracy that current models cannot deliver. We propose treating AI responses not as outputs to be trusted but as inputs to be processed-noisy signals that, when combined with real human outcome data through supervised learning, substantially improve behavioral prediction. We develop a formal framework establishing when and why this works and derive five testable implications. Using consumer willingness-to-accept data from a social media discontinuation experiment with two LLM generations (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.1), our method reduces prediction error by 66-86% relative to naive substitution and by 59-72% relative to single-signal linear correction. Decomposing these gains, we show that calibration, multi-signal combination, and nonlinear estimation each contribute substantially. All five implications are supported. Most strikingly, GPT-4.1-a far worse direct predictor than GPT-3.5 (RMSE .520 vs. .231)-yields nearly identical final prediction quality (.075 vs. .077), demonstrating that recoverable information content, not AI accuracy, is what matters.</jats:p>

items.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into robotic systems, their potential to generate socially and culturally appropriate affective touch remains largely unexplored. This study investigates whether LLMs-specifically GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and GPT-4o --can generate culturally adaptive tactile behaviours to convey emotions in human-robot interaction. We produced text based touch descriptions for 12 distinct emotions across three cultural contexts (Chinese, Belgian, and unspecified), and examined their interpretability in both robot-to-human and human-to-robot scenarios. A total of 90 participants (36 Chinese, 36 Belgian, and 18 culturally unspecified) evaluated these LLM-generated tactile behaviours for emotional decoding and perceived appropriateness. However, existing approaches often introduce security vulnerabilities, as they rely only on token‐based analysis, and most existing models were developed for specific programming languages. This study develops an enhanced vulnerability detection framework that incorporates a graph‐based representation and a tokenized representation for effective vulnerability detection across multiple programming languages. An enhanced vulnerability detection framework is proposed in this study that leverages code property graphs (CPGs) and graph attention networks (GATs) to capture structural code relationships, while byte pair encoding (BPE) and CodeT5+ perform token‐level vulnerability detection. The fusion of graph‐based and token‐based representations improves accuracy in identifying security flaws such as buffer overflows, injection attacks and memory leaks. To evaluate the efficacy of the proposed vulnerability detection framework, we conducted an experimental study on three vulnerability datasets. The three datasets detect the vulnerabilities with an accuracy of 96.71%, 98.80% and 95.84%. This shows that the proposed model effectively detects vulnerability across multiple programming languages.</jats:p>

title: From Argumentation to Labeled Logic Program for LLM Verification
items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) often generate fluent but incorrect or unsupported statements, commonly referred to as hallucinations. We propose a hallucination detection framework based on a Labeled Logic Program (LLP) architecture that integrates multiple reasoning paradigms, including logic programming, argumentation, probabilistic inference, and abductive explanation. By enriching symbolic rules with semantic, epistemic, and contextual labels and applying discourse-aware weighting, the system prioritizes nucleus claims over peripheral statements during verification. Experiments on three benchmark datasets and a challenging clinical narrative dataset show that LLP consistently outperforms classical symbolic validators, achieving the highest detection accuracy when combined with discourse modeling. A human evaluation further demonstrates that logic-assisted explanations improve both hallucination detection accuracy and user trust. The results suggest that labeled symbolic reasoning with discourse awareness provides a robust and interpretable approach to LLM verification in safety-critical domains.</jats:p>

title: Explainable Graph Learning for Vulnerability Detection with LLM-Generated Program Flows
items.abstract: <jats:p>Software vulnerabilities pose significant risks to the security and reliability of modern software systems. Graph-based vulnerability detection methods have demonstrated strong performance by leveraging program representations such as Control Flow Graphs (CFGs) and Data Flow Graphs (DFGs). However, constructing these graphs typically relies on static analysis tools, which require complex language-specific parsing and analysis pipelines and may be less effective when processing incomplete or syntactically incorrect code. In this paper, we investigate the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) for generating CFGs and DFGs directly from source code. We evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs, namely GPT-4o, GPT-4.1-nano, and DeepSeek-V3, and compare the generated graphs against ground-truth graphs constructed using Joern. Experiments are conducted on the OWASP and Juliet Java datasets and the BigVul C/C++ dataset. GPT-4o produces quality graphs that are structurally closest to the Joern baseline across both graph representations. Results demonstrate that GT achieves performance close to the Joern baseline when trained on GPT-4o-generated graphs, indicating that LLM-generated CFGs and DFGs can effectively support graph-based vulnerability detection. Furthermore, we investigate the explainability of GT predictions using GNNExplainer, Grad-CAM, and Integrated Gradients (IG). The generated explanations are quantitatively evaluated using Graph Explanation Faithfulness (GEF) and Graph Explanation Stability (GES). Across both Java and C/C++ datasets, IG consistently provides the most faithful and stable explanations. Overall, the results demonstrate the feasibility of using LLM-generated program graphs for graph-based vulnerability detection while supporting reliable and interpretable model explanations.</jats:p>

title: How AI Stereotypes the World: Regional Narrative Templates in LLM-Generated Stories
items.abstract: <jats:p>Prior work has shown that large language models generate a single dominant narrative structure across stories prompted with different national identities, a form of structural bias distinct from previously studied representational bias. Using a publicly released dataset of 11,800 stories spanning 236 nationalities, we apply sentencetransformer embeddings and regional centroid analysis to ask a finer-grained question: does narrative homogenisation operate uniformly across all 236 nationalities, or does the model impose different stereotyped templates by world region? We find that homogenisation is not uniform. Assigning each nationality to one of five UN M49 geographic regions and computing one centroid per region from 384dimensional story embeddings, we measure each story's cosine similarity to all regional centroids. The resulting confusion matrix reveals five distinct regional narrative templates with an overall match rate of 74.7%. Critically, the Africa-Asia cross-regional conflation (12.8% and 14.0% in both directions) is the largest off-diagonal entry by a factor of approximately 1.5× over any other cross-regional pair, providing a quantified instance of what postcolonial scholars term the "undifferentiated Other." Europe achieves the highest narrative self-coherence (83.6%), consistent with the documented Western-centric alignment of large language models. Regional vocabulary analysis via TF-IDF contrast reveals that cultural encoding operates almost entirely through character names and one or two iconic landscape features, with narrative arc converging across all regions. We additionally document the failure of KMeans clustering (silhouette scores 0.031-0.039 for K = 4. .. 20), informative in itself: the embedding space has no discrete cluster structure, only continuous variation with regional pull.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) have been widely adopted to assist in IoT device code development. However, prompts are typically provided by the user and adjusted based on the user's judgment when the generated code fails to function as expected. As a result, users often have to test candidate solutions one by one. In this paper, we propose an on-device development model that dynamically adjusts prompts based on on-device validation results and device parameter retrieval, creating a closed-loop process for code development. The process begins with the user providing requirements and device-specific information to the LLM, which generates both functional and validation code. The generated code is validated directly on the device by the model. If the code fails continuously beyond a specified threshold, the model iteratively refines the prompt by modifying its scope and word order. Furthermore, candidate solutions from the LLM are organized into a tree structure, enabling the efficient reuse of common steps across solutions. The results show that prompt adjustments based on device parameters and validation enhance accuracy, while the tree structure approach improves the efficiency of testing candidate solutions by 25%.</jats:p>

title: Observer-Mediated Multi-LLM Triangulation: Human-Routed External Verification Without Inter-Model Deliberation
items.abstract: <jats:p>When multiple large language models are consulted on the same question, agreement is often treated as evidence of reliability. That inference is weak when models share training data, development pipelines, or alignment methods, and a divergence-triggered procedure cannot address identical correlated errors. This paper isolates a narrower, tractable object: the procedural interval between visible inter-model divergence and final decision. We develop Observer-Mediated Multi-LLM Triangulation (OMT), a low-machinery verification procedure. Models are queried separately, without access to one another's outputs and without debate, critique, or synthesis. Their divergences are preserved and classified before cross-exposure. A human observer selects decision-relevant divergences and routes each, by type, to grounding independent of the output chain under review. The verification chain ends with the return of grounding, not a synthesized verdict; final adoption is a separate, recorded human judgment. OMT retains five authorities on the human side: salience, routing, sufficiency, stopping, and final adoption. Each is assigned to a named decision-maker, with dispositions and stated grounds recorded. Cases with no observed divergence, or no selected divergence, close as screening prefixes and do not certify agreement. Because the observer is fallible, the method requires observation-condition logging and, in repeated deployment, an error-model ledger that includes both human and model failure modes. The paper defines the constitutive conditions, verification stages, provenance requirements, risk tiers, and failure modes of OMT. Four author-reported development episodes motivate the framework but do not validate it. OMT does not claim superiority over deliberation protocols or improved decision accuracy. Its designed contribution is narrower: to make the path from divergence to external grounding, and from grounding to adoption, attributable and inspectable.</jats:p>

title: LLM-Aided Verification Gap Detection: A Methodology for Identifying Missing Checkers in UVM Testbenches

affiliation.name: Independent Researcher

items.abstract: <jats:p>High code coverage does not guarantee complete verification. Coverage metrics measure where tests exercise the design, but not whether outputs are actually checked. This gap between exercising code and validating results-the verification gap-allows bugs to escape even with 99%+ coverage. When outputs differ between correct and faulty RTL, but all tests still pass, checkers are missing. This paper presents a novel methodology for identifying verification gaps through LLM-aided analysis of mutation-induced behavioral divergence. The approach combines automated fault injection with structured LLM prompting to systematically detect missing checkers that coverage metrics cannot reveal. The theoretical foundation rests upon a constructive proof: injection of semantically non-equivalent mutations into golden RTL, followed by differential simulation, exposes precisely those output behaviors that evade checker scrutiny. The workflow is straightforward: (i) introduce a small change (mutation) to the RTL, (ii) run the same tests on both original and mutated versions, (iii) if outputs differ but tests pass, a gap exists, (iv) use an LLM to suggest the missing checker, and (v) validate the fix. The entire detection cycle takes about 80 seconds per mutation. Proof-of-concept validation on two representative IP blocks-a round-robin arbiter (350 LOC, algorithmic complexity) and synchronous FIFO (150 LOC, numeric boundaries)-demonstrates methodology feasibility: 4× time reduction, 100% precision (zero false positives), and cross-domain applicability across distinct fault morphologies. Break-even analysis yields N * ≈ 10 faults for initial deployment with asymptotic reduction to N * ≈ 2 upon amortization. The results establish feasibility of LLM-aided gap detection as a complement to traditional coverage-driven verification.</jats:p>

title: A scale for detecting LLM-generated responses in online survey research

affiliation.name: Princeton University

items.abstract: The rise of LLM-generated respondents poses a growing threat to the integrity of online survey research, yet available detection techniques remain opaque, proprietary, or poorly matched to the problem. In the present project, we propose and evaluate ECLAIR (Exploiting Common Limitations of AI Respondents), a novel framework for developing AI-detection items. We generated synthetic respondents using six LLMs (NTotal = 1,800) and compared them to census-matched samples of human participants recruited from five online data-collection platforms (NTotal = 1,518). Using a set of common tasks and scales drawn from the social sciences (e.g., the Trolley Problem; the Cognitive Reflection Test), we found that response distributions produced by synthetic respondents and human respondents diverge substantially, such that a researcher who relied solely on the former would be liable to misestimate experimental effects and systematically underestimate individual differences. Critically, we also found that a set of 22 items designed using the ECLAIR framework could successfully discriminate between the two types of respondents (AUC = .990), correctly classifying 98.78% of synthetic respondents and 95.78% of human respondents. A cross-validated short-form of four items preserved much of this accuracy (AUC = .980), correctly classifying 97.78% of synthetic respondents and 96.05% of human respondents. Although this project demonstrates that synthetic respondents pose a serious threat to online survey research, it also shows that novel tools, such as the ECLAIR framework, can help mitigate that threat.

title: Reliability of LLM-generated Optimization: A Critical Review of Models, Algorithms, and Decisions
items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models generate optimization formulations, algorithms, and operational decisions. A successful solver run or a matching objective value does not by itself establish that the generated output is correct. This review asks what reliability claims the literature supports, which assumptions those claims require, and how the checks themselves are evaluated. We conduct a critical narrative review of work available through September 2026, organizing studies by the output checked, the property claimed, the evidence used, the trusted inputs, and the instances covered. We distinguish numerical agreement, behavioral testing, formal certification, statistical selection, and safeguards that restrict an output's effect. The evidence reveals three recurring limitations. A guarantee about a formal object does not validate its translation from a user's requirements. Agreement among candidates need not expose a shared specification error. Empirical success on selected instances does not establish performance throughout a problem class. Reported checks also leave unresolved cases or reject correct outputs, but their rates have different denominators and cannot be pooled into a single reliability estimate. We compare the available evidence across formulations, algorithms, and direct decisions; clarify the difference between benchmark-label agreement and model correctness; and develop an evaluation protocol with explicit error rates, coverage, reference quality, and computational budgets. The review identifies research opportunities in independently checkable formulation benchmarks, distribution-specific evaluation of generated policies, and execution rules with proved loss bounds. Its contribution is an evidence-based account of what current checks establish and what additional evidence is needed before operational use.</jats:p>

title: Examining and Addressing Barriers to Diversity in LLM-Generated Ideas
items.abstract: <jats:p>Ideas generated by independent samples of humans tend to be more diverse than ideas generated from independent LLM samples, raising concerns that widespread reliance on LLMs could homogenize ideation and undermine innovation at a societal level. Drawing on cognitive psychology, we identify (both theoretically and empirically) two mechanisms undermining LLM idea diversity. First, at the individual level, LLMs exhibit fixation just as humans do, where early outputs constrain subsequent ideation. Second, at the collective level, LLMs aggregate knowledge into a unified distribution rather than exhibiting the knowledge partitioning inherent to human populations, where each person occupies a distinct region of the knowledge space. Through four studies, we demonstrate that targeted prompting interventions can address each mechanism independently: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting reduces fixation by encouraging structured reasoning (only in LLMs, not humans), while ordinary personas (versus "creative entrepreneurs" such as Steve Jobs) improve knowledge partitioning by serving as diverse sampling cues, anchoring generation in distinct regions of the semantic space. Combining both approaches produces the highest idea diversity, outperforming humans. These findings offer a theoretically grounded framework for understanding LLM idea diversity and practical strategies for human-AI collaborations that leverage AI's efficiency without compromising the diversity essential to a healthy innovation ecosystem.</jats:p>

title: StepCache: Step-Level Reuse with Lightweight Verification and Selective Patching for LLM Serving

affiliation.name: Lincoln University

items.abstract: We address LLM serving workloads where repeated requests share a common solution structure but differ in localized constraints such as output schema, variable names, or numeric constants. Prior caching approaches typically reuse either full responses (semantic caching) or model-internal KV/prefix states, which are brittle under partial changes or tightly coupled to specific backends. We present StepCache , a backend-agnostic step-level reuse layer that segments outputs into ordered steps, retrieves the best matching cached request, verifies steps using lightweight task-aware checks, and regenerates only failing regions through selective patching. StepCache also supports strict structured-output enforcement for JSON through single-step extraction, required-key constraints, and one-shot repair, and includes conservative skip-reuse fallbacks for semantic changes. For linear equations, StepCache promotes verification into correction via a bounded repair loop with a deterministic fallback that guarantees correctness when the backend model fails. In a CPU-only perturbation-heavy micro-benchmark on math and JSON variants (10 base prompts per task with 3 variants per perturbation, totaling 222 evaluation requests per seed), averaged over three seeds (42–44), StepCache reduces mean latency from 2.13 seconds to 0.67 seconds (median: 2.42 seconds to 0.01 seconds; p95: 3.38 seconds to 3.30 seconds), reduces total token usage from 36.1k to 27.3k (162.7 to 123 tokens per request), and improves end-to-end correctness from 72.5% to 100% under both task-specific checks and a stitched-output integrity check. Across requests, 79.7% take the reuse-only fast path, 5.4% require patching, and 14.9% trigger skip-reuse.

title: Silent Implementation Shortfall in LLM-Written Trading Code
items.abstract: <jats:p>Traders increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) to turn a strategy described in desk language into executable code. We measure the cost of that translation. Holding the strategy, the price path and the frictions fixed, we compare a reference implementation with the implementation an LLM writes from the same description; the return difference is an implementation shortfall attributable to translation alone, with the strategy’s own alpha differenced away. Across equity index and cryptocurrency markets, most programs written by low-cost models run without error yet depart from the authorised behaviour, and the median absolute shortfall ranges from several hundred to over two thousand basis points of initial equity. The sign of the average shortfall varies across models and samples, so the loss is better described as unpredictable deviation than as a haircut. The shortfall is larger for strategies whose risk logic carries state for longer, but this gradient is explained by holding duration: within a given type of risk control, models do not diverge more often on longer-state logic, and each divergence costs more the longer the strategy stays in position. We find no robust evidence that volatility amplifies the loss, and errors are close to independent across strategies, so the risk is largely diversifiable. Frontier models still diverge silently on more than a quarter of tasks, and neither compilation, backtesting nor an LLM code review detects the divergence.</jats:p>

title: ChainBench: An LLM Benchmark for Cross-Chain Code Generation
items.abstract: <jats:p>AI agents are increasingly capable of repositoryscale software work, and smart-contract engineering is a particularly high-stakes setting where toolchains and tests enforce correctness. We introduce ChainBench, a benchmark for cross-chain smart contract translation and contract generation built from production repositories and their real verification suites. Each task provides a structured specification and containerized environment: systems implement missing functionality to pass the existing verification suite, and are scored by Pass@1 task success. ChainBench contains 42 tasks spanning EVM Solidity, NEAR Rust, Aptos Move, Sui Move, and Starknet Cairo. In a zero-shot evaluation of nine deployed modelagent systems, including both standardized sameharness runs and preferred-harness runs where available, the best achieves 88.1% success, while several open-weight systems reach 52%-60% with substantially longer solve times. Performance further varies by target chain and task type, with failures ranging from narrow behavioral mismatches (e.g., missing edge-case guards) to build and repository-compatibility issues.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Quick Response (QR) codes are now widely used as a digital communication tool. However, their extensive adoption has made them an attractive target for cyberattacks, particularly through the injection of malicious URLs that redirect users to phishing sites or initiate malware installations. Conventional security approaches such as blacklists and antivirus software are no longer efficient against such evolving threats. This vision paper proposes an AI-based framework using fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify malicious URLs embedded within QR codes. To ensure transparency, a novel ensemble Explainable AI (XAI) is applied to aggregate insights from various XAI methods to explain the features influencing model predictions, facilitating more robust interpretations. To enhance clarity and usability, the proposed framework incorporates personalized explanations tailored to cybersecurity analysts, system developers, and non-expert end users, informed by a role-specific user study. Furthermore, as XAI methods may expose sensitive model behavior, cyberattackers craft adversarial inputs to mislead the model or manipulate explanations. This necessitates the integration of adversarial training to ensure model robustness and explanation integrity, evaluated through perturbation consistency checks. The paper outlines key challenges in explanation fidelity and personalization and presents a development roadmap to advance secure, transparent, and human-centric explainable QR code analysis.</jats:p>

title: No Test, No Claim: Untested Code is Vibed Code Verification as the Price Signal of Correctness
items.abstract:
<jats:p>When a large language model writes code we do not trust, we tend to blame the author: a machine wrote it, so it must be suspect. This paper argues that the instinct points at the wrong variable. What makes code trustworthy is not who wrote it but whether reproducible evidence exists that it does what it claims. 
<br>
<br>
 Authorship is inert; verification is everything. We defend one thesis -<b>&nbsp;untested code is vibed code, whether a human or a model wrote it</b> - and build it as a single argument rather than a tour of disciplines. 
<br>
<br>
 We begin where the argument is strongest: a correctness claim about untested code has no content. It is an unsigned promise (Design by Contract), an unfalsifiable assertion (Popper), and, in Alf Ross's sense, a <b>tû-tû</b> -- a bookkeeping word that connects a wish to a reliance while denoting nothing in between - because the theory that would give it content, in Naur's sense, never leaves the author's head. 
<br>
<br>
 Authorship cannot supply that content: a private, perishable understanding is, on Nozick's truth-tracking account, a belief that would persist even if the code were broken, which is to say not knowledge at all, and&nbsp; the human author and the model collapse into the same case. A program's real 
<br>
 law is its behavior in execution - the legal realists' <b>law in action</b> - not the <b>paper rules</b> of its names, types, and comments; the test is the court decision that discloses it. What running on vibes costs is then contested ground: the cost splits cleanly into a part that can be priced and a part that 
<br>
 cannot. 
<br>
<br>
 Chicago prices the first (the Learned Hand formula renders a cheap omitted test negligent by construction; the market for lemons explains why 
<br>
 untested modules cannot be told from working ones); Austrian marks the limit of the second (the calculation problem; dispersed, tacit knowledge) -- and the test is what a decision-maker needs at exactly that boundary, the decentralized feedback signal that substitutes for a global correctness calculation no one can perform. We make the cost concrete with a compound-Poisson actuarial model, of which the Hand formula is the point-estimate special case, and an estimable panel specification, then bound its pretensions with the Austrian caveat that its parameters are guesses at a moving target. The practical contribution follows from that model. Because operational-risk capital under Basel II and Solvency II is itself a 
<br>
 compound-Poisson loss distribution, a test is an operational-risk control with a measurable effect on regulatory capital; the Learned Hand formula is the deterministic point estimate of that model's pure premium; and the industry's faith in "battle-tested" code systematically under-reserves the tail in which latent security failures -- Dirty COW, the XZ backdoor -- actually live, because production tenure samples the body of the loss distribution and never it's tail. 
<br>
<br>
 Under every step the same verdict returns, and none of them can find authorship on the relevant side of the ledger. 
<br></jats:p>

items.abstract: Due to the use of the current power line network, Power Line Communication (PLC) technology has recently received a lot of attention. Because power lines are designed to transfer electric power at low frequencies, they are not appropriate for high-speed data transmission. The main problem with PLC is Impulsive Noise (IN). In PLC, the Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) approach is used to reduce the impact of IN. To prevent the occurrence of a higher level of channel impulsiveness, MIMO’s success in reducing IN is insufficient. It’s necessary to use further IN reduction techniques. In this study, cyclic redundancy check assisted successive cancellation list (CRCSCL) polar coding and the minimum mean square error (MMSE) detector techniques are combined to reduce the IN effect in MIMO-PLC systems with various antenna configurations. By comparing various degrees of channel impulsiveness, the Bit Error Rate (BER) performance under the Middleton Class A (MCA) and Bernoulli Gaussian (BG) IN models is examined. The obtained findings show that, in comparison to the BG model, the suggested IN mitigation under the MCA noise model requires a low Signal to Noise Power Ratio (SNR) value. Similar to this, the results show that more MIMO-PLC configurations, a higher level of channel impulsiveness in the MCA of the impulsive index (A), a higher Gaussian to IN average power ratio (Γ), and a lower occurrence of IN probability (P) over the BG would all enhance MIMO-PLC system performance.

<jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in enterprise software development workflows for source-code generation, debugging, documentation, test creation, refactoring, and design assistance. While these systems improve productivity and reduce repetitive programming effort, their deployment in enterprise environments introduces significant risks related to insecure code suggestions, hallucinated functionality, non-compliant logic, weak explainability, dependency misuse, and over-reliance by developers. This research paper investigates how LLM-assisted code generation can be made secure, reliable, and trustworthy through a structured governance-oriented framework that integrates prompt constraints, retrieval support, policy-based filtering, automated validation, secure coding guardrails, and human-in-the-loop review.

Drawing only on the provided literature, the study positions enterprise code generation within the broader development of LLMs, code-specialized models, hardware generation models, design automation agents, and AI-assisted engineering workflows. Prior work on GPT-4, StarCoder, CodeGen2, Magicoder, VerilogEval, RTLLM, OpenLLM-RTL, ChipNeMo, ChipGPT, AutoChip, and secure hardware generation demonstrates that LLMs can generate technically meaningful artifacts but remain vulnerable to correctness gaps, evaluation instability, insufficient domain grounding, and security-sensitive errors (Achiam, 2023; Li, 2023; Nijkamp et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2023; Thakur et al., 2023). This paper extends those insights to enterprise software engineering and proposes a Trustworthy Secure Code Generation Framework organized around six layers: task specification, retrieval-augmented contextualization, constrained generation, security-policy enforcement, validation and testing, and accountable human approval.

The findings suggest that trustworthiness in LLM-assisted enterprise code generation cannot be achieved by model scale alone. Instead, it requires layered controls that combine technical verification, organizational policy, developer accountability, and continuous feedback. The proposed framework reduces the probability of insecure code propagation, improves explainability of generated outputs, supports compliance-oriented review, and transforms LLMs from autonomous code producers into controlled development assistants. The paper concludes that enterprise adoption of LLM-assisted coding should prioritize measurable trust, secure-by-design workflows, traceable decision-making, and hybrid human-AI governance.</jats:p>

title: Is AI-Generated Code Faster Than Human Code? An Execution-Time Comparison Using the HumanEval Benchmark
items.abstract: <jats:p>A common assumption in green/sustainable software engineering discourse is that AI-generated code may carry a hidden efficiency cost relative to human-written code. This paper tests execution-time efficiency using the HumanEval benchmark (Chen et al. 2021), whose 164 tasks include genuine human reference solutions, enabling a true, task-level paired comparison against AI-generated completions for identical prompts. We generated completions using Claude Sonnet 4.5, filtering to functionally correct solutions only (verified via HumanEval&apos;s own test harness): 164/164 (100.0%) human and 159/164 (97.0%) AI solutions passed. Our original design specified direct hardware energy measurement via Intel RAPL counters, but we confirmed this interface is unavailable both on native Windows and inside WSL2 on the measurement machine, a documented hypervisor-level limitation; we disclose this transparently and pivot to execution time, a well-precedented proxy when direct energy measurement is unavailable. Using a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test on 159 task-level pairs, AI-generated solutions execute significantly faster than human solutions on average (mean 0.831ms vs. 1.363ms; p=0.0331). Because execution-time means are sensitive to measurement noise, we conducted five robustness checks; four confirm significance, with the median-based test showing an even stronger effect (p=0.0061) and a bootstrap 95% confidence interval ([0.007ms, 1.470ms]) excluding zero. We discuss this finding&apos;s scope, the honest limitations of a single-model, single-benchmark, execution-time-only design, and directions for future work using direct hardware energy measurement.</jats:p>

title: The Contracts Not Written: Measuring Covenant Tightness with LLM-Generated Synthetic Counterfactuals
items.abstract: <jats:p>Syndicated loan covenants exhibit substantial heterogeneity even among observably similar borrowers. We ask whether this variation reflects economically meaningful differences in contracting outcomes shaped by bargaining power or is largely incidental once observable risk is accounted for. Using a new measure of covenant tightness, defined as a contract's position within a deal-specific distribution of feasible covenant packages generated by large language models and validated against independent programmatic methods, we document a sharp asymmetry across borrower credit quality. Among investment-grade borrowers, tighter covenants are associated with significantly higher loan spreads but do not predict subsequent violations. Among speculative-grade borrowers, tightness has no incremental pricing power but strongly predicts violations. This cross-outcome asymmetry is difficult to reconcile with a residual risk interpretation and instead reflects two distinct contracting regimes: negotiated outcomes driven by bargaining power for investment-grade borrowers, and lender risk management and proximity to binding constraints for speculative-grade borrowers. More broadly, we show how counterfactual contract distributions can be used to measure contract design in settings with substantial contractual heterogeneity.</jats:p>

title: Stereotypes in the Machine: Gender and Racial Bias in LLM-Generated Financial Advice
items.abstract: <jats:p>We conduct a large-scale controlled experiment of large language models (LLMs) acting as financial advisors. We find that LLMs systematically recommend lower equity allocations to female and Asian clients compared to otherwise identical White males. This bias persists and even intensifies for financially sophisticated investors, rejecting rational statistical discrimination in favor of stereotyping. While higher model intelligence mitigates these biases, standard safety alignment and explicit debiasing prompts prove ineffective. Our results suggest that without advanced reasoning capabilities, AI advisors risk institutionalizing wealth disparities by projecting demographic stereotypes onto investment decisions.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Android malware continues to evolve through obfuscation and polymorphism, posing challenges for both signature-based defenses and machine learning models trained on limited and imbalanced datasets. Synthetic data has been proposed as a remedy for scarcity, yet the role of Large Language Models (LLMs) in generating effective malware data for detection tasks remains underexplored. In this study, we fine-tune GPT-4.1-mini to produce structured records for three malware families: BankBot, Locker/SLocker, and Airpush/StopSMS, using the KronoDroid dataset. After addressing generation inconsistencies with prompt engineering and post-processing, we evaluate multiple classifiers under three settings: training with real data only, real-plus-synthetic data, and synthetic data alone. Results show that real-only training achieves near-perfect detection, while augmentation with synthetic data preserves high performance with only minor degradations. In contrast, synthetic-only training produces mixed outcomes, with effectiveness varying across malware families and fine-tuning strategies. These findings suggest that LLM-generated tabular malware feature records can enhance scarce datasets without compromising detection accuracy, but remain insufficient as a standalone training source.</jats:p>

title: Calibrating LLM-Generated Sentiment and Risk Signals for Risk-Aware Reinforcement Learning Trading
items.abstract: <jats:p>Risk-aware reinforcement learning has shown promise for portfolio management, but the role of LLM-generated financial signals remains unclear: strong textual signal injection may improve responsiveness, but may also amplify noise and destabilize trading behavior. This paper studies how pre-computed LLM-generated sentiment and risk scores should be calibrated when integrated into CPPO-based trading agents. Building on FinRL-DeepSeek, we first analyze the sensitivity of policy performance to the strength of LLM signal integration. We then introduce a bounded Phase 1 modulation mechanism that applies neutral missing-value handling, sentiment/risk normalization, confidence weighting, turbulence attenuation, asymmetric sentiment sensitivity, and smooth multiplicative action adjustment. Experiments on Nasdaq-100 assets over 2019-2023 show that weak LLM integration performs best overall, with CPPO-DeepSeek 1% approximately matching the passive Nasdaq-100 benchmark while improving downside-risk metrics. The proposed Phase 1 mechanism does not dominate this simpler configuration, but improves vanilla CPPO on downside-risk metrics such as drawdown and CVaR. Because the LLM signals are inherited from an existing dataset and cannot be fully audited for point-in-time validity, the contribution should be interpreted as a controlled study of signal-integration mechanisms rather than as evidence of deployable LLM-based trading profitability.</jats:p>

title: Beyond Accuracy: How Content Format Shapes User-Perceived Helpfulness of LLM-Generated Answers
items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude increasingly function as primary information intermediaries, synthesizing content from the web into direct, conversational answers. While research on LLM output quality has concentrated on factual accuracy and hallucination, far less attention has been paid to the form in which information is presented and to how this form shapes user-perceived helpfulness. This paper addresses that gap through a blind comparative evaluation in which experienced AI users performed forced-choice judgments between content-format variants of LLM-generated answers. Three mainstream systems (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude) each generated responses in four format conditions (continuous prose, FAQ, fact list, table) to twenty realistic information-seeking prompts. Participants were blinded to both system identity and format category. Analysis is based on 2,160 evaluation decisions from 36 participants. Results reveal systematic, system-specific format preferences: FAQ dominates strongly for ChatGPT. Prose narrative is the preferred format for Gemini. Claude responses are perceived as helpful across formats with a comparatively flat preference distribution. Across all three systems, tabular formatting is consistently the least preferred. These findings suggest that perceived helpfulness constitutes a distinct quality dimension alongside factual accuracy. Content creators, enterprises, and public-sector information providers can influence these dimensions directly through the structural choices they make on their own web properties. We discuss implications for human-centred design of LLM interfaces and for emerging content-provisioning frameworks such as answer engine and generative engine optimization.</jats:p>

title: From PLS to Support Vector Methods: Auditable LLM-Generated R Workflows for Spectroscopic Chemometrics ​
items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) can substantially reduce the time and programming expertise required to develop chemometric workflows for spectroscopic data, but the reproducibility of LLM-generated analyses depends on the methodological specifications provided to the models. This study evaluated whether LLMs can generate auditable and reproducible R workflows for both qualitative and quantitative spectroscopic analysis and examined the use of support vector methods as nonlinear alternatives to partial least squares (PLS)-based approaches. Two spectroscopic datasets were investigated. The first comprised ATR-FTIR serum spectra from adult Wistar rats classified as sham-operated controls (SHAM) or ovariectomized (OVX) animals. PLS discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) and radial basis function support vector machine (RBF-SVM) were used for qualitative classification. Because PLS-DA showed substantial overlap between the classes, RBF-SVM was subsequently optimized using cross-validation. The second dataset comprised 11,691 near-infrared spectra of mango fruit with reference dry-matter measurements. Partial least squares regression (PLSR) and radial basis function support vector regression (RBF-SVR) were used for quantitative prediction. All workflows were independently generated by ChatGPT and Gemini, and the resulting R scripts were executed without modification. The scripts explicitly documented data processing, spectral preprocessing, model construction, validation, hyperparameter optimization, and performance evaluation, allowing each computational step to be inspected and reproduced. RBF-SVM provided improved classification relative to PLS-DA for the FTIR dataset, demonstrating the potential advantage of a nonlinear support-vector approach when class separation is not adequately represented by a latent-variable model. For mango dry-matter prediction, PLSR provided stronger overall predictive performance, whereas optimized RBF-SVR produced lower absolute bias, demonstrating that the nonlinear method can provide a complementary modeling strategy rather than a universal replacement for PLSR. Importantly, independently generated workflows from ChatGPT and Gemini produced highly consistent results when preprocessing, model parameters, validation procedures, and performance criteria were explicitly specified. The use of two independent LLMs therefore provides an additional cross-model consistency check, while the availability of the complete R scripts enables code-level auditing of the analytical procedures. These results demonstrate that LLMs can generate useful and auditable chemometric workflows within seconds, but reliable LLM-assisted spectroscopy requires explicit methodological specification and critical verification of the generated code and analytical results.​</jats:p>

title: In AI We Verify? Literacy, Privacy Concerns, and Task Importance in Verifying LLM- Generated Information
items.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into everyday information-seeking and decision-making contexts, concerns have grown regarding their tendency to produce inaccurate or fabricated outputs, such as hallucinations. This study investigates factors associated with users’ intention to verify LLM-generated information, focusing on three domains: user competencies (digital literacy, information literacy, and AI literacy), sociotechnical attitudes (trust in AI and privacy concerns), and usage characteristics (frequency of use and perceived task importance). Analysis of a survey of U.S. adult LLM users shows that AI literacy is the strongest and most consistent predictor of verification intention: individuals with higher AI literacy report greater intention to verify LLM outputs, including cross-checking information, requesting supporting evidence, and reporting inaccurate information to LLM platforms. Digital literacy shows a positive but smaller association with verification intention, while information literacy is not significantly related. In addition, higher privacy concerns and greater perceived task importance are positively associated with verification intention, although these effects are smaller in magnitude compared to AI literacy. These findings provide valuable initial evidence about user-level factors that shape information verification behaviors in human-AI interaction, addressing one of the pressing concerns in increasingly AI-mediated information environments.

We used a dataset of student-written text in comparison with LLM-written text. We leveraged several ML and Deep Learning (DL) algorithms, such as Random Forest (RF) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and utilized Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to understand the important features in attribution. Our method is divided into (1) binary classification to differentiate between human-written and AI-generated text and (2) multi-classification to differentiate between human-written text and text generated by five different LLM tools (ChatGPT, LLaMA, Google Bard, Claude, and Perplexity). Results show high accuracy in multi- and binary classification. Our model outperformed GPTZero (78.3%), with an accuracy of 98.5%. Notably, GPTZero was unable to recognize about 4.2% of the observations, but our model was able to recognize the complete test dataset. XAI results showed that understanding feature importance across different classes enables detailed author/source profiles, aiding in attribution and supporting plagiarism detection by highlighting unique stylistic and structural elements, thereby ensuring robust verification of content originality.</jats:p>

title: CoT+ (Chain-of-Thought Extended): A Reproducible Multi-Reasoning Prompting Architecture for Deterministic PLC Code Generation
items.abstract: <jats:p>Generating production-grade Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) code using Large Language Models (LLMs) presents a critical challenge: ensuring the determinism and safety required for industrial environments. Current baseline prompting methods, such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Program-of-Thought (PoT), Chain-of-Code (CoC), and Contrastive CoT (CCoT), often yield fragmented results that lack the structural integrity needed for safety-critical IEC 61131-3 synthesis. This paper introduces CoT+ (Chain-of-Thought Extended), a unified prompting architecture that integrates these four paradigms into a deterministic, multi-stage pipeline.The novelty of this research lies in its rigorous three-layer validation framework, utilizing Human-in-the-Loop (HITL), LLM-in-the-Loop (LITL), and Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) score analysis. To provide "double justification" for the superiority of CoT+, we employ an advanced Inter-Rater Reliability (IRR) assessment using Cohen’s (κ) for pairwise agreement and Krippendorff’s (α) for multi-rater consistency. This dual-layered statistical approach ensures that performance gains are not only observable across lexical and semantic layers but are also mathematically robust and validator-agnostic. Our results demonstrate that CoT+ achieves significantly higher safety compliance and cross-validator stability than existing baselines. This research contributes: (i) a deployment-oriented prompting template for industrial PLC synthesis, and (ii) a fully reproducible, IRR-qualified validation methodology designed for external verification in safety-critical domains.</jats:p>
